title: Why a cleansing coming is not absurd
source_text: Εἶτ᾿ ἐπεὶ προσωποποιεῖ ἰδίᾳ μὲν Ἰουδαίους αἰτιολογοῦντας τὴν κατ᾿ αὐτοὺς μέλλουσαν Χριστοῦ ἐπιδημίαν ἰδίᾳ δὲ Χριστιανοὺς λέγοντας περὶ τῆς ἤδη γεγενημένης ἐπιδημίας εἰς τὸν βίον τῶν ἀνθρώπων τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ· φέρε καὶ ταῦτα, ὡς οἷόν τε ἐστὶ, διὰ βραχέων κατανοήσωμεν. Ἰουδαῖοι δὴ παρ᾿ αὐτῷ λέγουσι πληρωθέντα τὸν βίον πάσης κακίας δεῖσθαι τοῦ καταπεμπομένου ἀπὸ θεοῦ, ἵν᾿ οἱ μὲν ἄδικοι κολασθῶσι, τὰ δὲ πάντα καθαρθῇ ἀνάλογον τῷ πρώτῳ συμβάντι κατακλυσμῷ. ἐπεὶ δὲ λέγονται καὶ Χριστιανοὶ τούτοις προστιθέναι ἕτερα. δῆλον ὅτι καὶ τούτοις φησὶ ταῦτα λέγεσθαι. καὶ τί ἄτοπον ἐπὶ τῇ χύσει τῆς κακίας ἐπιδημήσειν τὸν ἀποκαθαροῦντα τὸν κόσμον καὶ ἑκάστῳ κατ᾿ ἀξίαν χρησόμενον; οὐ γὰρ κατὰ τὸν θεὸν ἐστι μὴ στῆσαι τὴν τῆς κακίας νομὴν καὶ ἀνακαινῶσαι τὰ πράγματα. ἴσασι δὲ καὶ Ἕλληνες κατακλυσμῷ ἢ πυρὶ τὴν γῆν κατὰ περιόδους καθαιρομένην. ὡς καὶ Πλάτων που οὕτω λέγει· „ὅταν δ᾿ οἱ θεοὶ τὴν γῆν ὕδασι καθαίροντες κατακλύζωσιν, οἱ μὲν ἐν τοῖς ὄρεσι“ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. λεκτέον οὖν ὅτι ἆρ᾿ ἐὰν μὲν ἐκεῖνοι ταῦτα φάσκωσι, σεμνά ἐστι καὶ λόγου ἄξια τὰ ἐπαγγελλόμενα, ἐὰν δ᾿ ἡμεῖς τάδε τινὰ ὑπὸ Ἑλλήνων ἐπαινούμενα καὶ αὐτοὶ κατασκευάζωμεν, οὐκέτι καλά ἐστι ταῦτα δόγματα; καίτοι γε οἷς μέλει τῆς πάντων γεγραμμένων διαρθρώσεως καὶ ἀκριβείας πειράσονται δεικνύναι οὐ μόνον τὴν ἀρχαιότητα τῶν ταῦτα γραψάντων ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν σεμνότητα τῶν λελεγμένων καὶ τὸ ἀκόλουθον αὐτοῖς.
pass_a_gloss: Then, since he personifies/dramatises (προσωποποιέω) on one side (ἰδίᾳ μέν) Jews giving the cause/reason (αἰτιολογέω) of the coming (ἐπιδημία) of Christ which according to them is about to be (μέλλουσα), and on the other side (ἰδίᾳ δέ) Christians speaking about the already-happened (ἤδη γεγενημένη) coming into the life (βίος) of men of the Son of God (υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ): come (φέρε), let us also consider (κατανοέω) these, as far as possible (ὡς οἷόν τε), briefly (διὰ βραχέων). Jews, then, in him (παρ᾿ αὐτῷ) say the life, having been filled (πληρόω) with all wickedness (κακία), needs (δέομαι) the one being sent down (καταπέμπω) from God, so that the unjust (ἄδικοι) may be punished (κολάζω) and all things be purified (καθαίρω) analogously (ἀνάλογον) to the first flood (κατακλυσμός) that happened (συμβαίνω). And since Christians too are said to add (προστίθημι) other things to these, it is clear he says these things are said by these too. And what is absurd (ἄτοπον), at the outpouring (χύσις) of wickedness, that the one who will cleanse thoroughly (ἀποκαθαίρω) the world (κόσμος) and will treat (χράομαι) each according to worth (κατ᾿ ἀξίαν) will come (ἐπιδημέω)? For it is not according to God (κατὰ τὸν θεόν) not to stop (ἵστημι) the spreading (νομή) of wickedness and to renew (ἀνακαινόω) the affairs (πράγματα). The Greeks too know (οἶδα) the earth being purified periodically (κατὰ περιόδους) by flood or fire, as also Plato somewhere says thus: 'whenever the gods (οἱ θεοί), purifying the earth with waters, flood (κατακλύζω) it, those in the mountains' and the following. It must be said (λεκτέον) therefore: is it that if those say these things, the things announced (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) are solemn (σεμνά) and worthy of account (λόγου ἄξια), but if we too establish (κατασκευάζω) some of these things praised (ἐπαινέω) by Greeks, these doctrines (δόγματα) are no longer fine (καλά)? And yet those to whom the articulation/clear exposition (διάρθρωσις) and exactness (ἀκρίβεια) of all the written things matters will try to show not only the antiquity of those who wrote these things but also the dignity of the things said and their consistency.
pass_b_english: Next, he brings on stage, on one side, Jews who explain the reason for the coming of Christ, a coming that in their view still lies in the future, and on the other side, Christians who speak of the coming of the Son of God into human life as something that has already taken place. Come, then, let us look into these points too, as briefly as we can.

The Jews in his book say that human life, filled with every kind of wickedness, needs one sent down from God, so that the unjust may be punished and all things purified, as in the first flood (compare Genesis 6:11–13; Genesis 7:21–23). And since the Christians too are said to add other things to these, it is plain that he says these things are said by them as well.

And what is absurd in this, that when wickedness has overflowed, one will come who will cleanse the world and deal with each according to what each deserves? For it does not befit God to leave the spread of wickedness unchecked and not to renew the order of things. The Greeks, too, know of the earth being cleansed at set periods by flood or by fire, as Plato also says somewhere: “Whenever the gods cleanse the earth with waters and flood it, those in the mountains…” (Plato, Timaeus 22d), and the rest.

We must ask, then: if the Greeks say these things, is what they proclaim solemn and worth a hearing, but if we too argue for some of these very things that the Greeks praise, are these doctrines no longer good? And yet those who are concerned with setting out clearly and exactly all that has been written will try to show not only the antiquity of those who wrote these things, but also the dignity of what they said and its consistency.

'not worthy of God' to 'does not befit God' (κατὰ τὸν θεόν); 'renew things' to 'renew the order of things' (τὰ πράγματα)

προσωποποιεῖ rendered 'brings on stage' (Celsus voices imaginary speakers). The Jews' claim is reported indirectly in the Greek, so it is kept as indirect speech without quotation marks. 'τὴν κατ᾿ αὐτοὺς μέλλουσαν Χριστοῦ ἐπιδημίαν' taken as 'the coming of Christ, still future in their view'. 'τῷ πρώτῳ συμβάντι κατακλυσμῷ' is a clear allusion to the Genesis flood, cited as 'compare'; 'πληρωθέντα τὸν βίον πάσης κακίας' echoes Genesis 6:11–13 (the earth filled with wickedness). 'οὐ ... κατὰ τὸν θεόν ἐστι μὴ στῆσαι ... καὶ ἀνακαινῶσαι' has a double negative: it does not befit God not to stop evil and not to renew things; rendered 'it does not befit God to leave ... unchecked and not to renew'. νομή is the medical term for a spreading sore, rendered 'spread'; χύσις rendered 'has overflowed'. 'ἑκάστῳ κατ᾿ ἀξίαν χρησόμενον' may recall Romans 2:6 or Matthew 16:27 ('to each according to his works'), but the wording differs, so no inline citation. 'ἀνακαινῶσαι τὰ πράγματα' may recall Revelation 21:5; uncertain, not cited. The Plato quotation is Timaeus 22d (the Egyptian priest on periodic floods and fires); Origen gives only the opening words and 'and the rest'. In 'ἐὰν μὲν ἐκεῖνοι ταῦτα φάσκωσι' the pronoun ἐκεῖνοι refers to the Greeks just named, so the English names them to avoid confusion with the Jews. λεκτέον introduces a question and is rendered 'We must ask'. 'τῆς πάντων γεγραμμένων διαρθρώσεως' rendered 'setting out clearly ... all that has been written', with no word added for what the writings are (context: the writings of Moses and the prophets).
